evidence.excerpt: Active packaging systems incorporating volatile antimicrobial agents derived from plant extracts represent a promising complement to conventional modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) for fresh blueberries. This study assessed the efficacy of sachets containing encapsulated thymol and carvacrol — sourced from wild thyme and oregano — integrated into clamshell packaging under a 5% O₂/15% CO₂ atmosphere at 2 °C. Blueberry quality was monitored over 18 days for firmness, total anthocyanin content, weight loss, and microbiological load (total aerobic count and Botrytis incidence). Active MAP sachets reduced total aerobic counts by 1.8 log CFU/g relative to passive MAP controls at day 12 and delayed visible mold onset by four days. Anthocyanin retention was significantly higher in active MAP treatments (p < 0.05), suggesting a secondary antioxidant protective effect. Consumer acceptability scores obtained through a 40-member sensory panel confirmed marketable quality at day 14 for saline-active MAP versus day 10 for passive MAP controls. Migration testing confirmed that thymol and carvacrol residues in fruit tissue remained below European regulatory thresholds. This work demonstrates the practical feasibility of combining MAP gas composition with natural antimicrobial active elements for export-grade blueberry packaging.
